Tanzania's GNI per capita, Atlas method (World Bank, 2024) is USD 1,210 (~USD 100.8/month). A subsistence 30 kWh/month on the D1 lifeline tariff costs roughly USD 1.1-1.2, i.e. ~1.1-1.3% of monthly GNI per capita — which alone would suggest 'Affordable (1-2%)' (code 4). But a peer-reviewed household survey (Muhihi, 2024, International Journal of Research in Community Studies) directly measuring the Price-Income-Ratio for 30 kWh/month subsistence consumption found real-world expenditure shares of 0.9-4.8% across income quintiles, with the lowest and medium quintiles spending roughly 3-5% of household income — pointing instead to 'Moderate (3-5%)' (code 3). The two credible calculation methods (theoretical lifeline-tariff-vs-GNI vs measured household-survey PIR) bracket the boundary between codes 3 and 4 rather than converging on one, so no single code is asserted here; this is flagged for human review rather than guessed. Codes 1, 2 and 5 are clearly ruled out by all evidence.
revised_comments: Residential electricity in Tanzania is priced on a tiered tariff structure regulated by EWURA (Energy and Water Utilities Regulatory Authority). The lowest 'D1' lifeline tariff charges TZS 100 per kWh for the first 75 kWh consumed per month, rising to TZS 350 per kWh above that threshold, while the general 'T1' tariff for domestic and small-business customers not on the lifeline block is TZS 292 per kWh (EWURA Fact Sheet, December 2025). Tanzania's GNI per capita is approximately USD 1,210 per year, or around USD 101 per month (World Bank, Atlas method, 2024). A household consuming the subsistence level of 30 kWh per month entirely on the lifeline tariff would spend roughly 1-1.5% of monthly income on electricity. A peer-reviewed household consumption survey (Muhihi, 2024) measuring actual expenditure shares for 30 kWh/month subsistence consumption found that most income quintiles spend between roughly 3% and 5% of household income, reflecting real-world tariff exposure above the minimum lifeline block for many consumers, while wealthier households spend under 1%. Electricity affordability in Tanzania therefore sits at the boundary between 'affordable' and 'moderately expensive' depending on actual household consumption levels and income group, with typical residential consumers spending in the low single digits of their income on basic electricity needs.
